questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the phrase "can vikfgt" (लोहे का पक्षी) in the poem, and what is the ironic gap between this label and the reality of the object it describes?
questions.a: The literal meaning is "a bird made of iron," referring to an airplane. The ironic gap is that a bird is a living, breathing creature born of nature, while the airplane is a dead machine manufactured by humans; calling it a bird elevates a mechanical object to a status it cannot truly possess — it has no instincts, no nest, no mate, and no freedom. A wrong answer that only defines "iron bird" as "airplane" without contrasting it with a real bird's qualities shows the student misses the irony's core: the mismatch between label and essence.

questions.q: In the dialogue, the child asks the iron bird: "vkidk vikfgtiu rks nq[k nsrk gksxk nsrk gS?" (Does your bird-ness give you pain?). Explain why this question is an instance of verbal irony, and what it reveals about the speaker's attitude toward the airplane.
questions.a: The question is verbally ironic because the speaker knows the airplane cannot feel pain — it has no consciousness — yet asks as if it could, mocking the very idea that a machine could share a bird's sensory experience. It reveals the speaker's (and poet's) skepticism: the airplane's "bird-ness" is a hollow performance. A wrong answer that treats the question as a genuine inquiry about the airplane's feelings shows the student cannot detect tone and takes the dialogue at face value.

questions.q: Apply the concept of symbolism: The poem describes the iron bird as having "cgqr cM+h rlohj" (very long wings) and "mlosQ gksaBksa ij ,d dlelkgV" (a pilot on its shoulders). What do these physical details symbolize about modern technology, and how do they contrast with the real bird's description in the following lines?
questions.a: The long wings symbolize technology's massive, imposed scale — it dominates the sky not by grace but by brute engineering. The pilot on its shoulders symbolizes human control and exploitation: the machine carries a human operator, unlike a bird that flies for itself. In contrast, the real bird is "n'kZd" (small), "èkhjt jf[k" (tender wings), and flies with its mate ("gesa nksuksa ,d lax jQykus gSa") — symbolizing organic harmony, partnership, and self-determined freedom. A wrong answer that only describes the physical details without linking them to abstract ideas (scale, control, freedom) shows the student treats symbols as mere decorations.

questions.q: Analyze the situational irony in the poem's closing image: the iron bird flies "ijns ij oDr dh dher gS" (there is a mountain of garbage on the earth) while the real bird and the child stand together on that same polluted ground. How does this spatial arrangement deepen the poem's critique?
questions.a: The situational irony is that the "superior" iron bird escapes the garbage-strewn earth by flying high, yet it is the very agent of the industrial civilization that produced that garbage. The real bird and the child, seemingly "inferior" because they remain on the ground, actually share a grounded truth: they witness the damage together. The iron bird's flight is not liberation but abandonment. A wrong answer that says "the airplane flies high so it is free" misses the irony that its freedom is built on the earth's degradation.

questions.q: Evaluate the poet's choice to frame the entire poem as a conversation between a child (or children) and the iron bird. Why is this dialogic structure more effective for conveying irony and symbolism than a direct descriptive poem would be?
questions.a: The dialogue forces the iron bird to "speak" and defend itself, exposing its emptiness when it cannot answer basic questions about its nest, mate, or feelings. The child's innocent questions act as an ironic mirror: each question reveals a quality the machine lacks. A descriptive poem would tell us the airplane is not a bird; the dialogue makes us hear the airplane's silence. A wrong answer that says "dialogue makes it interesting" without linking the structure to the devices' function shows the student cannot evaluate authorial craft.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in Hindi that uses irony and symbolism to contrast a natural river with a concrete canal, modeled on the poem's technique of giving the artificial object a false natural name (e.g., "can nadI" — iron river).
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) name the canal with a false natural label (e.g., "simInt kI nadI"), (2) give it an ironic voice claiming to be a river, (3) use a symbol (e.g., "no fish in its womb," "fixed concrete banks") to show its lifelessness, and (4) contrast with the real river's freedom/messiness. Example: "simInt kI nadI bolI main hUñ gangA / mÙke machlI nahIñ, kInAre haiñ saMgA / behtI nahIñ, bas rukI hUñ ek ḍhAAcA / aslI nadI hãsTÌ hai: 'tU to bas rAsTA bnA'." A poor answer that just describes a canal without irony or symbolic contrast shows the student cannot generate the devices independently.
